title: Santa Ana Swiss Water® Decaf
body:
This Swiss Water Decaf from our farms in El Salvador delivers on all fronts to be as rich, smooth and delicious as its fully caffeinated counterparts. The Santa Ana is a lighter, more dynamic roast, with sweet, vibrant notes of dried fruit, rich nougat, with a robust and chocolatey cacao nib finish.
Over the years, we have sourced dozens of different decaf lots from origins around the world, and though we’ve found some truly remarkable offerings, traceability remains an issue. After participating in the James Hoffman decaf project, we were able to learn a lot about the different decaf processes available and how they affect the flavor of the coffee in question. This gave us a perfect opportunity to retool our decaf program, and after over a year of research, development, coordination, and immense effort, we are very proud to have accomplished something truly remarkable in the specialty coffee industry. For the first time ever, we sent a container of coffee from our farms in El Salvador to the Swiss Water Decaffeination Plant in Vancouver, British Columbia, to have our very own direct trade, single origin decaf coffee.
This project has required an immense amount of collaboration from our team in El Salvador, our team here in Tulsa, and the good folks at Swiss Water in Vancouver. ABOUT THIS COFFEE AND PRODUCER
Wilder Lazo is actually a veterinarian specialized in livestock farming. As coffee prices continued to decline in 2016 and his father fell seriously ill, he decided to bring the family farm into the modern era with his brother. Initially, their coffees scored between 80-83 points on the cupping scale, despite elaborate processes and preparations. Wilder started examining soil samples and using targeted nutrients and fertilizers to neutralize the pH value, thereby increasing the availability of nutrients for the coffee trees. He refers to this as precision agriculture.
La Dinastía farm is where Wilder planted his first Geisha trees. He got seeds from Colombian farms, Panamanian farms and friends from Costa Rica. He planted all of them together and purified the genetics, eliminating trees that didn’t match the flavor profile he likes, or that produced very low yields.
For the yellow honey gesha, Wilder picked the ripe cherries and floated them in water to remove impurities. Then he dry-fermented them in cherry for 36 hours before de-pulping them and transferring them to the drying beds. title: Peak Reserve - Premium Microlot
body:
Peak Reserve encompasses the most premium coffee available from our farming communities. Each offering is a uniquely roasted micro batch crafted with meticulous attention to detail and quality. The quality of these beans is a substantial step above most of the coffee available on the market.
Our Current Microlot Selection : Ethiopia Natural from The Guji Region
The Dhaka Bor Banti Cooperative is located in the Kercha area of the Guji region of Ethiopia, at elevations ranging from 2,000 to 2,550 meters above sea level. The Guji zone is high in the mountains of Ethiopia and is an area rapidly gaining recognition within the country's already world-renowned coffee landscape. Their natural processed lots are known for clean, floral aromatics, bold fruit notes, and a syrupy, full texture.
This coffee has tasting notes of raspberry and blueberry mixed in with caramel and clove.
Despite Ethiopia's coffee exports accounting for nearly 60% of the national GDP, many coffee farmers and their families live in dire poverty with very limited access to education, health care, and water. Cooperative structures like Dhaka Bor Banti help smallholder farmers access specialty markets and fair trade pricing.
Enjoy this coffee while it lasts!
From the roaster : I am extremely excited to introduce our new line of incredibly exceptional coffees. Through our long term partnerships with farming cooperatives of various regions in Africa, we have been offered access to some of the world's finest coffees.

title: Ethiopia Geisha
body:
In the southwest corner of Ethiopia near the village of Gesha, in an area of very little deforestation, grew one of the most magical varietals of coffee for hundreds of years without notice. It was essentially undiscovered until 2004 when it was brought to Panama for cultivation and ended up winning the Cup of Excellence, making news all over the industry. This newly discovered varietal tasted of flowers, sweetness, berries. Over the next several years it sold for $100 a pound or more. Everyone wanted to try it. Soon, Guatemala started growing it, and with their alitude and climate, their crops tasted even better then what Panama was producing. Then Colombia and Costa Rica got into the Geisha market, both with great success. In the past few years, the price has fallen to about $20 a pound as more and more is available in the markeplace.
Just a few kilometers east of the village of Gesha is another small village called Bebeka. The Bebeka Village decided to start growing the Gesha varietal for commercial sale, and instead of it being the washed process that all the Central American countries are using, they used the dry process (natural) on their African drying beds. They then sorted and sorted and sorted it until it met a Grade 1 quality (almost unheard of for natural process coffee). To have a Geisha from its native land of Ethiopia, processed naturally, and sorted to perfection, is a really special experience. It is absolute top shelf coffee by any standard or comparison.
Us

title: A Small Porch – by Wendell Berry (Paperback)
body:
More than 35 years ago, Wendell Berry began spending his sabbaths outdoors, when the weather allowed, walking and wandering around familiar territory, seeking a deep intimacy only time could provide. These walks sometimes yielded poems. Each year since, he has completed a series of these poems dated by the year of its composition.
This new sequence provides a virtual syllabus for all of Berry’s cultural and agricultural work in concentrated form. Many of these poems were written on a small porch in the woods, a place of stillness and reflection.
Recently Berry has been reflecting on more than a half century of reading, to discover and to delight in the poetical, spiritual, and cultural roots of his work. In The Presence of Nature in the Natural World , Berry’s survey begins with Alan of Lille’s 12th-century work, The Plaint of Nature . From the Bible through Chaucer, from Milton to Pope, from Wordsworth to the moderns, Berry’s close reading is exhilarating. Moving from the canon of poetry to the sayings and texts found in agriculture and science, we gain new appreciation for the complexity of the issues faced in the 21st century by the struggling community of humans on earth.
With this long essay appended to these new Sabbath Poems, the result is an unusual book of depth and engagement. A new collection of Wendell Berry poems is always an occasion for celebration, and this eccentric gathering is especially so.

title: Guatemala Huehuetenango
body:
In the Cup: Fresh lime, vanilla, peanut butter, and cacao nib flavors with tart acidity and a soft mouthfeel.
Process: Washed
Regions: Huehuetenango
Variety: Bourbon, Catimor, Caturra, Maragogype, Pache
Elevation: 1400–2200 MASL
Country: Guatemala
Harvest: December–May
Huehuetenango sits in Guatemala's western highlands, pressed right up against the Mexican border, and it's one of the most respected coffee regions in Latin America for good reason — altitude, reliable water, and traditional varieties. This lot comes from the Quetzal program, named for Guatemala's national bird and built so smallholder farmers can sell more of their harvest and earn more along the quality ladder. It's a mix of the region's common varieties — Bourbon, Caturra, Catimor, Maragogype, and Pache — grown between 1,400 and 2,200 meters, where cool nights slow the cherries down and make for a dense, hard bean.
Washing is the classic Guatemalan approach: cherries are depulped the same day or the next, fermented anywhere from 12 to 48 hours, washed clean of their mucilage, and dried on patios or raised beds. With the fruit stripped off before drying, what's left in the cup is what the bean built on the tree — cacao nibs and a rich peanut butter middle, a touch of vanilla sweetness, and a squeeze of fresh lime for tart acidity, all on a soft, easy body.

title: Día de los Muertos
tags: Frothy Monkey Día de los Muertos
coffee for Day of the Dead
body:
Every fall for ten years, the coffee we roast for Día de los Muertos has come from the same six mountain communities in the Sierra Sur of Oaxaca. Día de los Muertos falls on November 1 and 2, when families across Mexico build ofrendas and set out food, drink, and marigolds to welcome back the people they've lost, and Oaxaca is one of the places where the celebration runs deepest. Roasting a coffee from there each year is how we mark it.
Those communities organize as Sicobi, a cooperative founded in 2010 with GAIA, a group of biologists who had already spent decades working in Oaxaca. Around 500 growers farm 1,500 hectares between 1,300 and 1,900 meters, mostly Caturra, Mundo Novo, and Typica, under a shade canopy the communities protect by policy. Young technicians from each community, many of them students, visit the parcels through the season to map varieties and soil, collect quality data, and advise growers on picking and processing. That data shapes which lots meet export standards, and only a small share of the harvest does.
The coffee is fully washed, and growers ferment it in wooden tanks rather than the cement or steel you'll find at most washing stations. The Sierra Sur is unusually dry for coffee country, with hot days and cold nights that slow the cherry down as it ripens, and between the long ripening and the wooden tanks, Sicobi lots tend to come out sweeter and rounder than you'd guess from a washed coffee.

title: Panama Camiseta Estate
body:
The Baru Volcano is the highest mountain in Panama and has a surreal beauty. Orchids naturally grow in the wild, rainbows are always present, everything is a lush green, and it has a jungle-like feel to it. Birdwatchers, hikers, anthropologists, photographers, etc all enjoy the beauty of Baru Volcan.
Of course the coffee grown on the mountain is fantastic as well. Think of it as a Costa Rica, it has that balanced acidity, citrus undertone, and pleasant coffee taste. But it has an extra layer of complexity. Red apple, raisin, apricot, brown sugar, and flashes of other flavors appear and disappear as the coffee changes temperature while you're sipping at your mug.
Keep it out of the 2nd cracks. Even as you approach 2nd cracks, the bean has lost a lot of what makes it special. You really only want to take it about 25 seconds past the 1st cracks. On the lighter side of that range you get a tart coffee (but not grassy) where the apple and apricot flavors are pronounced and the acidity is on the higher end. Take it to the dark side of that range and you have more of the brown sugar, dried fruit flavors with a muted acidity. Right in the middle of it is our favorite -- it has a butter pecan/toffee sweetness covering a tart apple with medium zippy acidity. Very pleasant aftertaste, and overall, it tastes like normal coffee -- this isn't a natural processed fruit bomb or a bright citrus Kenya. Careful harvesting and traditional washed processing let the coffee’s natural character shine through, resulting in a cup that’s bright, elegant, and incredibly expressive.
Expect vibrant citrus, juicy stone fruit, and delicate florals with a silky sweetness that carries from the first sip to the finish. It’s the kind of coffee that keeps revealing something new as it cools.
If you’re looking for a clean, complex coffee that showcases why Ethiopia continues to set the standard for specialty coffee, this one’s an easy recommendation.

body:
ROASTING WEDNESDAYS WHILE SUPPLIES LAST
TASTING NOTES
﻿Aromas of toasted marshmallow, Green Apple and white grape. Boisterous acidity supported by flavors of meyer lemon and brown sugar. A Classic Breakfast cup.
Farm: Finca Cerro Azul
Variety: Ethiosar
Processing: Washed
Roast: Medium-Light
Background
The Mierisch Family has operated farms in Nicaragua for generations, planting their first coffee farm in 1908. Several years ago while judging the Cup of Excellence competition in neighboring Honduras, They were very impressed by the quality of the coffees and the altitudes available to growers here. They decided to purchase some land at high elevation: 1600-1700m and plant a selection of their best varieties from their farms in Nicaragua.
Ethiosar is a hybrid they brought back from Brazil a decade ago. Reported to be a cross of Rume Sudan x Sarchimor, back-crossed to Villa Sarchi which is one of the parents of the Sarchimor hybrid. This variety is currently limited to but a handful of farms and is produced in very small quantities. In early 2021 The Mierisch family held an online auction for their best cupping coffees from Their Nicaragua Farms. Judged by an international panel of experienced Cup of Excellence judges. An Ethiosar variety coffee ended up taking the top spot with a score of 90.30. A very promising variety in the cup that is also a very productive plant.

title: Julio Madrid - April
body:
MEET THE PRODUCER | Julio Cesar Madrid is a name you've seen on our menu before—he's the director of the joint farms, Finca La Riviera and Finca Milan, which were first cultivated by Julio's ancestors over forty years ago. Together with his business partner, Andres Julio Quinceno, Julio Madrid has made it his life's work to produce incredible coffees and practice innovative and exacting processing methods.
TRUST THE PROCESS | After being picked at peak ripeness, the coffee cherries are sorted for quality and density at the processing center before being placed in a temperature-controlled bioreactor alongside fermented peaches and pineapples, as well as a specially curated starter culture. The fermentation process lasts 36 hours, during which time the temperature is manipulated and the musto is recirculated. The coffee is then dried in a dark, temperature-controlled room outfitted with a dehumidifier, until optimal moisture content is achieved.
TAKE A SIP | This coffee is the belle of the cupping table season after season. Floral like jasmine and fruity like peach tea, it also features notes not often found in a mug, like melon and green grape. Everything about it feels delicate, elegant, and lovely.

title: Indonesia Java Blawan - Medium Roast
body:
Cupping notes : subtle dried apricot, pear, m edium acidity, big round body, slightly tea like, herbal, spicy, very balanced
Coffee cultivation in Indonesia holds a 300 year old story which has been significantly influenced by the Dutch colonization. Today Indonesia is the fourth largest coffee producer in the world. Approximately 85% of East Java Arabica coffees are owned and driven by PTP, standing for the official governmental organization that was founded in 1894 under the Dutch. The remaining 15% of the coffee production is in the hands of farmers that own very small plots of land using traditional processing techniques. Compared to other Indonesian coffees which are mostly semi-washed resp. wet-hulled, these estate coffees from Java including the Blawan and Jampit estates are fully washed. This processing has a significant impact on the flavor due to the fermentation process of approximately 36 hours. After drying the coffee down to a humidity content of approx. 12% the coffees beans are carefully hand-sorted leading to a very consistent and clean cup profile. The Blawan plantation covers a total of 1.250ha while Jampit plantation covers 1.400ha.
Interesting to note: Sumatra, Indonesia, Java, Papua New Guinea have fairly similar taste notes. Often they are 'earthy.' Many roasters go fairly dark, toward French [Full City] roasts for these regions. This is why many folks say these are "bold, strong." Kind of like you.

title: Rwanda Nyabumera
body:
When we bring in Rwanda coffee, we often try to find the chocolate-driven taste profile, with less acidity and less fruit.
This one likes to be roasted not quite to the second cracks. There's a fairly large window of ending temperature in this area where you will get good results, but for your first try, take it to the verge of 2nd cracks. We are getting strong chocolate and slight almond notes in it here. If you go a little lighter you get raisins and plum flavors dancing in the background. Juicy and complex. If you go lighter yet, you get lemongrass notes, which I feel like detracts from the enjoyment that the medium roast flavor offers.
This coffee comes from the Nyabumera washing station in the Nyamasheke District of Rwanda, operated by the COOPAC cooperative. This small lot comes from just two producers: Jean Ndagijimana and Angelique Nyirangendahayo.
Instead of being high acidity, thin bodied, and super fruity like our other Africans, this one is smoother, richer bodied. Makes for a really nice medium roast mug of coffee.

title: Ethiopia Royal Select Natural Decaf Coffee
body:
Ethiopia Royal Select decaf coffee , a natural process lot decaffeinated with the Mountain Water Process. Rounder and more chocolatey than our Sidamo, with dried berry and cocoa and a soft, sweet finish. Water only, no solvents.
Roasted to order in Concord, California and shipped within 72 hours. Available in 6 oz, 12 oz and 24 oz bags.
Ethiopia Royal Select decaf coffee is the friendlier of our two Ethiopian decafs. It is a natural process coffee, dried in the cherry, run through the Mountain Water Process in Mexico, which uses glacial water from Pico de Orizaba and no chemical solvents. The result keeps the Ethiopian fruit but leans sweeter and more chocolatey than the Sidamo. We roast it to order on our Buckeye roasters in Concord, California.
What Ethiopia Royal Select Decaf Coffee Tastes Like
Dried berry and cocoa up front, a jammy sweetness through the middle, and a soft finish with a hint of something floral. The body is medium to full. If the Sidamo is a bright blueberry, this one is blueberry jam on dark toast.
Royal Select is the designation for Mountain Water Process decafs, and the method is gentle. Green beans soak in pure water saturated with coffee solids so that caffeine migrates out through a filter while the flavor stays behind. It is a close cousin of the Swiss Water Process and gives a similarly clean result.
Origin and Region: Ethiopia, southern growing regions
Decaf Process: Mountain Water Process (MWP), Royal Select, water only
Altitude: 1,700 to 2,100

About the Farm
COOPAFSI (Cooperative Agraria “Frontera San Ignacio” Ltda) was officially established in June 1969. Gender equality was an important factor when the land was purchased and divided among producers. This particular cooperative is unique because they empower and promote “women grown” coffee. These women contribute to the physical and sensory quality of the coffee. They are always managing new projects and developing new ways to improve the lives of their families. They focus their efforts on improving quality and delivering consistent coffee to different markets. In 2016, a committee of women was created by the cooperative and they are responsible for distributing loans which will enable producers to improve their own land while also taking part in new developments for their kitchens, crafts and livestock. They also created a computer lab which allows all members to stay up to date with modern technology.

title: Finca El Sendero • Colombia
body:
This Roaster's Choice release marks Commonplace Coffee’s first time purchasing from Colombian coffee exporter Unblended . This coffee was selected by Commonplace Coffee’s Head Roaster, Erin Bloom!
Andrés Martinez is a Biochemical Engineer with coffee growing roots, leading him to pursue a career linked to the coffee world. Andrés began his coffee career at Tecnicafé, an institute dedicated to coffee research and innovation. He later joined the staff at Finca El Paraiso, one of the most famous farms in the world overseen by the legendary Diego Samuel Bermudez. At this farm, Andrés was in charge of soil studies and process standardization. Andrés’ experiences up to this point have given him a unique skill set to conduct highly complex experiments - all while maintaining a high standard and consistency at his farm, El Sendero, in Cauca.
The processing details for this coffee highlight his skill set and approach to experimentation very well. Initially, this coffee was hand harvested and floated in water to remove impurities. Then the coffee cherries were fermented in closed tanks with beer yeast for 48 hours. Next, the coffee was removed from these tanks and depulped, after which they undergo an additional 24 hour fermentation in closed tanks. The coffee was then dried on raised beds in 3 stages with increased sun exposure every 5 days, for a total drying period of 12 to 18 days depending on weather conditions.
This coffee is incredibly complex, clean, and vibrant with a vivid be

title: India Garige Khan Estate
body:
This is a shade grown estate coffee grown 3500 feet above sea level in the Muthodi Reserve Forest in Chikmagalur, Southern India.
All of the coffee produced at Garige Khan undergoes a washed process, utilizing the abundant water from streams and nearby lakes. The estate composts the by products generated from coffee bean processing and treats contaminated water to reduce environmental impact. Additionally, the estate provides fair wages, housing, sanitation, potable water, and medical care for both men and women.
This bean hits the exact profile I love tasting in a washed process India. It has a spicy vibe to it like cinnamon and corriander, plus some chocolate, so it's like a mexican hot chocolate. In really dark roasts, it tastes much like you would expect from a Sulawesi bean, with some spice and smokiness.
India is an underrated coffee. It is in close geographic proximity to Yemen and Africa, both of which command much higher prices for their coffees. Indian coffee has a clean, creamy taste that you would think would give it more credit in the coffee world, and often you find spicy notes in darker roasts and nutty notes in light roasts. What else would you expect from India? They grow coffee alongside their spices.
Sometimes I let it out right before the second cracks where I get a sweet nutty note, but usually I give it 15 seconds of 2nd cracks and pull it out as a medium-dark roast which is the best way to taste the spicy flavors. All in all, it is a versatile and forgi

Light Roast
Located in Bursa Woreda in the south of Ethiopia at elevations of 2,100 to 2,300 meters above sea level, Wasa works with local farmers who cultivate coffee using traditional methods and maintain a deep connection to their land. That close relationship is reflected in every cup, with each lot carefully processed to preserve the depth and character of the cherries delivered to the station.
Wasa is run by Daye Bensa Coffee, which opened the station in 2021 and works with about 240 farmers in the surrounding area. Daye Bensa was started by two coffee-producing brothers, Assefa and Mulugeta Dukamo, from the Bensa area of Sidama. More than 20 years on, it's one of Ethiopia's major coffee exporters, shipping green coffee from its own farms and from the farmers it partners with, across grades from conventional to specialty.

Dark Chocolate, Honey, Raspberry
Periscope is our rotating blend that explores two different coffee growing regions, blended to create a unique yet balanced flavor profile while retaining the distinctive character of each region.
This time, we are heading to South America, Central America, and Africa. We paired a sweet and full-bodied coffees from Brazil and Colombia with a lively coffee from Ethiopia. In the cup, the result is a well-balanced blend that is sweet, vibrant & complex. The citrus notes that characterize the Ethiopia cut through the sweet, chocolaty, and nutty tones of the Brazil and Colombia in a manner both subtle and distinct. Periscope is delicious as espresso and plays well with milk while being a superstar as a drip.

title: San Pedro Farmer Pin • Funding Ciro's Pink Bourbon Project
body:
Producer: Albiero Lugo
Project: Cherry Buying/Pink Bourbon
Goal: $10,000 raised
Region: Huila, Colombia
Albiero and his father Ciro have been some of our most valued partners for the last nine years. Industrious and exacting this father/son team carved an existence out of an area with almost zero specialty buyers for years, still focusing on quality. Ciro espoused the belief to his son and all their neighbors that quality was worth the effort within itself despite a lack of commensurate payment. We've been very proud to provide that commensurate payment over the years we've worked together and watched them reinvest heavily each year into quality and production.
This year Albiero is looking to expand his production, not through additional plants, but by purchasing pink bourbon from all his neighbors. We are able to pay a high price for this treasured variety, and some of the first farmers to plant it are here in the community of La Marimba. There's a lot of new infrastructure and startup costs required to expand into cherry buying, and his first focus is to build an additional drying area; a large raised bed greenhouse system referred to as a marquesina.
Support and accelerate Albiero's pink bourbon/cherry buying project with this coffee farmer pin designed by Zaine Vaun, one of our favorite illustrators !

title: HUEHUETENANGO | GUATEMALA
body:
Huehuetenango, Guatemala
Roast : Balanced
Process : Washed
Tasting Notes : Red Berry, Chocolate, Caramel
Varieties : Bourbon, Caturra
Elevation : 1,524-1,830 MASL
Ixlama comes from the department of Huehuetenango near the Guatemala-Mexico border, a region known for its rugged landscapes, high elevation, and for the 22 ethnic groups of Mayan descent who call this community home. This coffee is the culmination of work by approximately 120 family producers in the municipalities of San Pedro Necta and La Libertad. Many producers here identify as Maya, speak one of the seven local dialects, and work on their farms dressed in the colorful, hand-loomed textiles associated with their individual communities — a tradition that contributes to Guatemala's rich culture and to unique identity of this coffee-growing country.
Consisting of 50 percent Bourbon and 50 percent Caturra varieties, this coffee was grown at an elevation of 1,524 to 1,830 meters above sea level. Ixlama, a shade-grown coffee, is harvested and brought to Transcafe’s mill at Caserio Teogal Aldea San Martin. At the mill, located near the town of Todos Santos, coffees are sun-dried on cement patios for four days before being placed in “guardiolas,” a type of coffee dryer
patented by a Guatemalan resident in 1872. The coffees are then computer-sorted by color and separated by density mechanically, resulting in a superior, clean, and bright cup.

title: Cramp Bark ( cut & sifted)
body:
While the berries can be made into jam, the bark is often used in traditional European herbalism for its wellness supporting properties. Cramp bark is also referred to as guelder rose and is an important plant in Slavic folklore and art. The bark can be decocted, infused, or tinctured.
Viburnum opulus is a deciduous shrub in the Adoxaceae family. Native to Europe, the plant is now naturalized in North America. Cramp bark has white flowers resembling snowballs and clusters of red berries. While the berries can be made into jam, the bark is often used in traditional European herbalism for its wellness supporting properties. Cramp bark is also referred to as guelder rose and is an important plant in Slavic folklore and art. The bark can be decocted, infused, or tinctured.
Cramp bark is a large deciduous shrub growing as much as 15 feet (5 m) tall and 15 feet wide. It is native to the moist lowland forests of England and Scotland and naturalized to moist forests of the northern United States and southern Canada. The bark is stripped before the leaves change color in the fall, or before the buds open in the spring. A member of the honeysuckle family, cramp bark bears large white flowers, up to 5 inches (12 cm) across that yield red berries in the fall. The berries are eaten like cranberries, although moderation is recommended. Historically, the berries, once dried, have been used for making ink.

Varietal bourbon, pacas, catimor, caturra

El Milagro is for the medium roast drinkers. We found notes of chocolate babka, followed by raisin sweetness in the middle, and ending with some toasted walnut. It has the kind of mouthfeel that makes a cup feel substantial. On the cupping table it struck us as particularly chocolatey, and sweet without being delicate.

The lot blends Bourbon, Catimor, Caturra, and Pacas all grown around 1,100 meters. Pacas is a special Bourbon descendant first discovered in this same region! The washed process keeps the cup clean, so the chocolate and nut character the region is known for comes through without distraction.

body:
RWANDA | 1800 – 2200 MASL | RED BOURBON | ANAEROBIC NATURAL
This is the cream of the crop from the Nova Washing station. An anaerobic natural processed coffee which in 2024 won the best of Rwanda. While most of the Roastery Reserve coffees are best suited to pour over, this coffee is more diverse, making a vibrant espresso (1:2), an incredibly sweet Cortardo, and a a rich and fruity pour over (1:16). The Story
A proud partnership between Nova Coffee, Crop to Cup, and Coffeebar.
Nova Coffee is a Rwandan coffee company founded by a pharmacist Felix Hitayezu and his wife Agnes Mukamushinja (nurse) who apply the same precision and care to coffee as they do in healthcare.
Their Mission : Empowering local farmers—especially women—to grow top-quality coffee while improving their community’s well-being.
In 2017, Rwanda changed its coffee laws, requiring farmers to deliver cherries to specific mills and setting a minimum price to prevent exploitation. While meant to help farmers, this also took away their choice of where to sell, making it harder for some washing stations—like Nova—to get coffee.
Now, certifications like Fairtrade, UTZ, and Organic matter more than ever, shaping how Rwandan coffee is sold. While this ensures consistency, it also shifts focus away from pure quality. Despite these challenges, Nova Coffee continues to push for excellence and support their farmers.

title: Jasmine Bai Hao | Scented Green
body:
Hugo Tea's 2025 JASMINE BAI HAO hails from Guangxi province, China, a tea growing region known for heicha ("dark tea"). The province is also home to Heng county, famed for its jasmine flower production. Hugo's project tea producer at Long Kou tea farm (an unusually skilled green tea maker) leverages the fertile soils of north-central Liuzhou and the high fragrance flowers from neighboring Heng in his annual production of our house jasmine. The base tea is harvested in early spring (pre-Qing Ming) at a loose 1:4 (1 bud : 4 leaves) plucking standard, fixed, machine-disrupted into semi-pearls, and after the summer jasmine harvest, scented in 6 rounds.
Hugo Tea's take on this Fujian classic is produced in small lots with the intention of selling out by next harvest. Mingfu, the producer and Hugo's on-site liaison, takes his jasmine production very seriously—he's as much a connoisseur of fine wine as tea, and understands the value of a well-rounded bouquet that elevates the base tea (rather than masks it). Unusual in scented tea, this lot is rich with cha qi—Mingfu's low-intervention, middle-aged, da ye cultivar trees pack a punch.
To achieve a thorough but balanced scenting, hundreds of hand-plucked jasmine flowers mingle with the base tea overnight, are sorted and removed by hand, and the process repeated 6 times before being packed at origin. title: Brazil Sitio Mortadella
body:
This natural processed microlot from Brazil makes a fantastic shot of espresso. We roast it 15-20 seconds into the 2nd cracks (not as dark as our normal Brazil espresso roast) and end up with a shot of espresso that is chocolatly and creamy with tons of crema. When made as espresso, it has a rich, thick mouthfeel and grapefruit sweetness, but no bitterness. You could drink 10 of these if you weren't careful.
As coffee, we roasted it to the verge of second cracks and it was a very drinkable Brazilian coffee. It had a medium body, a similar grapefruit sweetness to the espresso and had some chocolate or toffee undertones. If you're looking for an affordable single estate bean for coffee or espresso look no further -- this is a phenomenal choice.
This Brazil came from one particular farm and is the two varietals they grow; Yellow Catuai and Yellow Caturra. They blended the two varietals this year because it tasted nicer than each coffee individually. It is very uncommon to be able to get that much information and traceability from a coffee coming from Brazil. At almost a mile above sea level this coffee is processed by Arari Bernardes, his wife Sandra and their two sons; Marco and Pedro in the south-east of Brazil. They dry it under the sun on long patios. This is a mircolot so there wasn't much of it to begin with and it's extremely fresh right now. We got lucky and grabbed it so that our customers can enjoy this wonderful Brazil.

Grown at 3000 – 4000 feet elevation, picked and naturally milled then dried mechanically. Harvested from April – September.
Cerrado is a region in the state of Minas Gerais, the largest coffee-producing state in Brazil. Coffee has been a major crop in this region since the 1980’s mainly because of the devastating black frost of 1975 that forced growers from the Parana region to relocate north to Cerrado and other areas of Minas Gerais. Today, coffee is produced by over 4,500 growers on 175,000 hectares of farmland with yields of approximately 5.5 to 6.0 million bags per year. The coffee is grown in rich soil that the natives call “Terra Roxa” or “Red Earth” and other factors such as consistent rains, high daytime temperatures, and dry winters combine to make the Cerrado region ideal for producing coffee.

title: Mystery and Manners: Occasional Prose (FSG Classics) by Flannery O’Connor
body:
This bold and brilliant collection is a must for all readers, writers, and students of American literature
When she died in 1964, Flannery O’Connor left behind a body of unpublished essays and lectures as well as a number of critical articles that had appeared in scattered publications during her lifetime. The brilliant pieces in Mystery and Manners , selected and edited by O’Connor’s lifelong friends Sally and Robert Fitzgerald, are characterized by the boldness and simplicity of her style, a fine-tuned wit, understated perspicacity, and profound faith.
The book opens with “The King of the Birds,” her famous account of raising peacocks at her home in Milledgeville, Georgia. There are three essays on regional writing, including “The Fiction Writer and His Country” and “Some Aspects of the Grotesque in Southern Fiction”; two on teaching literature, including “Total Effect and the Eighth Grade”; and four on the writer and religion, including “The Catholic Novel in the Protestant South.” Essays such as “The Nature and Aim of Fiction” and “Writing Short Stories” are gems. Their value to the contemporary reader–and writer–is inestimable.

Farm Description:
Papua New Guinea occupies the Eastern half of the island it shares with the Indonesian province of Irian (no sizable coffee production comes from Irian). There can be a huge range of cups from Papua New Guinea, and the so-called Plantation coffees represent the cleaner character of the coffee produced on the island... more like a good Central American than part of the Indonesian profile. This decaf is a good representation of the balanced flavors you can find in Papua New Guinea, and quite versatile in terms of roast level and brew methods. The lot is comprised of the coffee from many small farms in Goroka, which is part of the very high altitude Eastern Highland region. Coffee grows between 1700 and 2000 meters above sea level, and the farms are typically less than 1 hectare on average. It was decaffeinated by the folks at Swiss Water Decaf in Vancouver, Canada. Their water-only process method removes 99.9% of the caffeine from coffee without any chemical solvents. title: Papua New Guinea Kimel A
body:
Every 4 years, Papua New Guinea holds an election and it causes strife and tribal uprisings (sound familiar?) So every 4th year, the farmers prune their trees way back, knowing it will cause a lower harvest, but then the following year the tree is happy and gives a huge harvest. They want a low harvest in the election year because there is so much political uncertainty with unrest, exchange rates, customs, etc, it is easier to just lay low. All that to say, this was an election year, it was full of drama, the coffee harvest was less than half of normal, and now Papua New Guinea coffee will be in scarce supply for the next 6 months.
Brand new, deep bluish large uniformly sized beans. I roast it quickly and gently to a light 397 degrees, where its out of the 1st cracks by maybe 30 seconds, but nowhere near the 2nds. This gives it the full-mouthfeel character that I associate with fine New Guinea coffee. A really nice lingering aftertaste, hints of pineapple and mango, no earthiness, and very little acidity. There are less distinct undertones here than with some New Guineas. While the sweet smooth fruitiness is there, it’s hard to pick out anything distinct. Aftertaste is clean. The reason for this is that most PNG coffees are of the Jamaica Blue Mountain varietal, but the Kimel Estate uses Jamaica trees in addition to trees transplanted from Tanzania, Colombia, and others. This blend creates a taste that is a little different than other PNG offerings — sweeter but less pronounc

title: Chamomile
body:
Chamomile is an herb grown commonly in England, and somewhat successfully in the United States, but the most prized chamomile comes out of Egypt. Chamomile looks like a daisy, with white petals and a yellow center. When dried and steeped as a tea, this herb is prized for its flavor, aroma, and soothing properties. This full flowered organic certified Egyptian Chamomile tea is soothingly aromatic, calmly smooth, and peacefully subtle with floral and fruity notes. Traditionally, it is prepared at bedtime with honey to induce sleepiness. But it is a fine tea to drink at any time that you wish to calm down, feel peaceful, and just escape the craziness of your day. Chamomile tea can also be blended with lavender or peppermint. The lavender further enhances a sleepy state, whereas the peppermint enhances a soothing digestive aid/after-dinner tea experience.
Not to boast, but our chamomile is so much higher quality than everyone else's. A few times we ran out and tried to buy some from local organic markets and spice stores and grocery stores, and all of their chamomile was 2 to 3 times the price, and shriveled up and brown and tiny blossoms. Ours is vivid, fresh, big flowers. aromatic, it's such good chamomile. Not that we deserve any credit for any of it other than a finder's fee, but it's our third best selling tea because it's so nice. We have some customers who buy nothing but this from us.
Ingredients: Organic Egyptian Chamomile
Tasting Notes: Soothingly floral, pollen, sweet

title: Costa Rica Hacienda La Minita Estate
body:
Coffee Review: 94 points
Blind Assessment: Elegantly fruit-toned. Strawberry-guava, pistachio, lime zest, freesia, cedar in aroma and cup. Sweetly tart structure with vibrant, juicy acidity; full, syrupy mouthfeel. The finish centers around notes of strawberry-guava and pistachio with cedar undertones.
Notes: Produced at Hacienda La Minita entirely of the Caturra variety of Arabica, and processed by the honey method, in which the skin is stripped off the coffee fruit but some of the fruit flesh is left to dry on the beans. RamsHead Coffee Roasters is a family-owned company operated by Bozeman, Montana natives Patrick and Sarah Flemming that specializes in direct trade microlot coffees.
The Bottom Line: A delicate, balanced honey-processed Costa Rica cup with notes of tropical fruit and complex, pistachio-like nut tones.
Background: Hacienda La Minita has been a pivotal partner for RamsHead since 2017. In 2017 we began a search to buy more coffee through farm direct models. La Minita along with the Menendez Estate in El Salvador became two of our primary buying partners and we never looked back.
For the past 4 years we have purchased exclusively a Honey Natural. This year we are changing our focus as we consider the current prices of the coffee market. For 2022 we have decided to purchase direct from the estate to make sure that we can maintain control over the quality of the coffee while paying a fair price to the farm, and offering coffee at a fair price to the market. title: India Arabidecool Estate
body:
This is a shade grown estate coffee grown 4000 feet up on the Baba Budangiri Mountain Range in Chikmagalur, Southern India. The two varietals of coffee grown on this estate are Kent (common in India but rarely grown elsewhere), and S-795 which was developed in India but is the primary varietal grown in Sulawesi and fairly common on the other Indonesian islands. This coffee does have a spicy finish much like you would expect from a Sulawesi bean. In a dark roast, it tastes almost exactly like a clean, well sorted, spiced Sumatra or Sulawesi.
India is an underrated coffee. It is in close geographic proximity to Yemen and Africa, both of which command much higher prices for their coffees. Indian coffee has a clean, creamy, nutty taste that you would think would give it more credit in the coffee world, and often you find spicy notes in darker roasts. This one has a definite spiciness to it. It’s not an earthy-tasting coffee, and it has a creamy and sweet grain-like quality to it in light to medium roasts. It reminds me of a combination of Chai tea and coffee. What else would you expect from India? They grow coffee alongside their spices.
Sometimes I let it out right before the second cracks where I get a sweet nutty note, but usually I give it 15 seconds of 2nd cracks and pull it out as a medium-dark roast which is the best way to taste the spicy flavors. Think clove and cinnamon and a little black peppercorn paired with the bold coffee taste and a little nutmeg and peanut. All i

title: Bare-Knuckle Espresso
body:
** Bronze medal winner at the Golden Bean North America roasting competition **
This is our flagship espresso at our own café. It's a beauty straight up, but it also punches through milk with sweetness and luscious viscosity.
So, what’s up with the name and the artwork? We named Bare Knuckle Espresso in honor of Richmond-born Tom Molineaux , a fascinating man born as a slave right here in Richmond, Virginia in 1784. Molineaux grew up to become a prolific boxer (all bare-knuckle at that time). He eventually earned his owner a large sum of money in winnings on bets, was granted his freedom, and moved to England where he expected to be able to earn money as a professional boxer.
He did have some success in the succeeding years, but never attained the wealth he had hoped for. Sadly, he died penniless — but free — in Galway, Ireland in 1818. That not withstanding, we are proud to honor the memory and legacy of a Richmond original — a man born into the ugliness of slavery who made his mark in his own way.
If you are an owner or an employee of a café that would like to put it through the paces at your own place, we’re always happy to send out samples. If you are an avid home barista who enjoys espresso a bit "off the beaten path" with fresh flavors, a balanced profile, and not a trace of the smoke you'd typically find in the majority of espressos, this will be right up your alley.

While the Arabica bean tends to be sweeter and smoother in taste with hints of sugar and chocolate, the Robusta bean has a stronger and bolder flavor in terms of bitterness. It also has a wonderful earthy aftertaste. The Chicory bean on the other hand has a thicker brew due to the starches and fiber roots that are a part of the bean along with a woody and nutty earthy tone that adds character to its flavor—combining all three of these delicious beans we give you the ‘Smell of Rain’. An earthy and spicy coffee with notes of smokey flavor that remind you and let you relive petrichor, the smell of rain. South Indian coffee such as our exclusive Smell of Rain is best brewed using centuries of history found exclusively in the South Indian Filter. This simple contraption allows for the coffee the percolate over 20 mins, 6 hours, or overnight, drop by drop, till it forms a rich ‘decoction’. Unlike an espresso shot, it is not recommended to drink the decoction directly, as it is much thicker with an almost syrup-like consistency. Instead, water it down with hot water if you’d like to drink it black, or do it the South Indian way – topped up with sweetened milk. Preparing authentic South Indian coffee at home is simple. Our Newest Dark Roast! From the rich volcanic soils of Guatemala, this dark roast features layers of rich dark chocolate, hints of strawberry, and a deep lingering finish.
Guatemala is home to some of the best soil and coffee growing conditions in the world, and is one of our favorite regions in the world. We are so incredibly excited to introduce this dark roast to our lineup!
We like to say that our craft is part artistry, part science, and a lot of luck! That was the case in finding this dark roast profile for this particular coffee. We had sourced this natural processed coffee as our light roast El Camino due to the strawberry notes and it has been a fan favorite. As part of our ongoing testing and experimentation with coffees, we took the coffee to a dark roast profile and were amazed with the change of characteristics and flavors the coffee underwent! It is now one of our favorite dark roasts that we've ever tasted.
About natural processed coffee: Natural process coffee is a coffee drying method where the coffee cherry is left to dry in the sun before the bean is removed. This process allows natural sugars and fruity notes from the cherry to seep into the bean, resulting in a coffee that has hints of fruit, and has a full-bodied, complex flavor.

This espresso is the default used for all espresso-based drinks and mocktails in our Flagship store. Recommended for espresso machine or MokaPot.
While espresso is an extraction method, many people believe that beans when grown are intended for espresso. That is not the case but as roasters, our job is to find characteristics of coffee (acidity, body, balance, aftertaste) that make a blend of coffees that compliment each other. title: Ethiopia Dumerso Yirgacheffe
body:
Dumerso is a private washing station located just north of the town of Yirga Chefe, in the heart of the coveted Gedeo Zone—the narrow section of highland plateau dense with savvy farmers and fiercely competitive processors whose coffee is known the world over as “Yirgacheffe.” As a coffee terroir, Yirgacheffe has for decades been considered a benchmark for beauty and complexity in arabica coffee—known for being beguilingly ornate and jasmine-like when fully washed, and seductively punchy and sweet when sundried.
The station now employs over 400 individuals during harvest season, 95% of whom are women. During harvest farmers deliver ripe cherries daily to the Dumerso mill. Last harvest they achieved both organic and Rain Forest Alliance certification for the station, and they are currently undertaking a project to establish a local plant to convert coffee parchment into a kind of pressed firewood, as a way of boosting income for the station to distribute to growers and to help local farmers rely less on local forests for their daily source of fire.
Sourced by InterAmerican Coffee Importers. Whole bean.

title: Berk’s Beans Africa – Single Origin
body:
African single origin coffee from Ethiopia, Kenya, Burundi, Rwanda, Tanzania, Uganda and Zambia. Expect fruit, florals and a bright, wine-like acidity you will not find anywhere else. Choose your lot and roast level, or leave it to Roaster’s Choice. Roasted to order in Concord, California and shipped within 72 hours in 6oz, 12oz, 24oz and 5lb bags.
African single origin coffee is the one that changes people’s minds about what coffee can taste like. Blueberry, jasmine, black tea, lemon, ripe apricot. It is what these beans do when they are grown at altitude and roasted with a light hand. Pick a lot below, pick a roast, and we roast it after your order lands.
What Makes African Single Origin Coffee Different
Two things. First, the varieties. Ethiopia in particular grows heirloom types found nowhere else, and they carry aromatics that other origins simply do not have.
Second, the processing. A lot of coffee here is dry processed, meaning the cherry stays on the bean while it dries. That pushes fruit and fermented sweetness deep into the cup. Washed lots from the same farms taste completely different, cleaner and more floral, so the process on the label matters as much as the country.
Acidity runs high across the region. Somewhere between a good merlot and strong black tea is the usual comparison. Body ranges from light and tea-like in Ethiopia to dense and syrupy in Kenya. If you have only ever had chocolatey coffee, African single origin coffee will read as bright at first. Giv

title: Guatemala La Morena Cubulco SHB
body:
Guatemala La Morena Program Green Coffee Beans
In 2016, the La Morena program was created to give female coffee growers access to the global supply chain and to address gender inequality in coffee farming. The program started off small; with four IWCA members to import 32 boxes of green coffee beans. It was a micro-lot by all accounts, but roasters were receptive, and the small lot quickly stocked out. The growers enjoyed success from that introduction to the market and their coffees and their coffees became highly sought after.
Fast forward to 2023: the specialty coffee sourcing team in Guatemala worked with over 800 women farmers spanning the coffee-growing regions of Huehuetenango and Baja Verapaz. What started as a micro-lot of about 2,000 lbs of coffee has blossomed into a platform that strongly addresses gender inequality in coffee. And roasters are thirsty for more!
About Baja Verapaz Cubulco
Baja Verapaz is one of Guatemala’s twenty-two departments. Within this central department is the municipality of Cubulco. Cubulco boasts numerous archaeological sites. The cultural heritage in Cubulco runs deep; the population, which is mainly comprised of indigenous people, continues to enjoy the customs passed down through generations. Meanwhile, paved roads to Guatemala’s capital, a tropical climate, high elevation and healthy waterways make Cubulco ideal for the cultivation of coffee.

title: ORIGAMI Wave (Flat Bottom) Filter Box
body:
The ORIGAMI wave-type paper filter is specifically crafted to pair with the ORIGAMI dripper. The ORIGAMI mix filter box features a unique wave design that perfectly matches the dripper's 20 ribs. By ensuring a snug fit, the filter minimizes gaps between the dripper and the paper, preventing water from bypassing the coffee grounds and optimizing extraction. This results in a more intense flavor profile, even during shorter brewing times.
The wave filter promotes a stable water flow, ensuring that water moves consistently through the coffee grounds. This balanced extraction process highlights the coffee's natural sweetness and body, without the risk of an over-extracted or bitter taste. Because the wave design creates a thinner coffee bed compared to traditional conical filters, water passes through more quickly, leading to even extraction from the top to the bottom of the grounds for a clean, balanced cup.
Crafted from natural pulp, the filter is designed to preserve the integrity of your brew, ensuring that no paper taste interferes with the coffee's nuanced flavors. The production process is meticulous, with filters pressed in small batches to reduce inconsistencies like wrinkles or folds. This attention to detail ensures a perfect fit with the ORIGAMI dripper, minimizing uneven extraction and allowing the coffee's true character to shine through.

CURRENT BLEND COMPONENTS | 80% Aricha – Washed | 20% Sebastian Ramirez – Red Fruits
They say you can't have it both ways.
Clean, vibrant, and approachable falls on one end of the spectrum, which is home to some of our first loves in coffee—Panamanian Gesha, washed Ethiopian lots, and breakfast blends. On the other end, you'll find our funky friends: anaerobic naturals, advanced processing experiments, and of course: our beloved co-ferments.
As roasters, baristas, and general coffee enthusiasts, asking us to pick a side between these two expressions of coffee gives us an impossible choice. So, we sought to create a year-round blend that showcases both, embracing innovation in fermentation and processing while simultaneously honoring those classic and storied flavor profiles.
This blend, which changes seasonally, will always be composed predominantly of a washed Ethiopian coffee. The minority percentage is then reserved for our party animal friends, the co-ferments. With each cup, you can expect to taste something fruit-forward and dynamic, but also clean and approachable. Our goal is to present you with a coffee that's both balanced and striking, traditional and innovative.
And, with all due respect to whoever they are, we hope this coffee will also persuade you to join us in proclaiming: actually, you can have it both ways, after all.

title: Shady Y Elias - Mixed Berry Ombligon
body:
MEET THE PRODUCER | For brothers Shady and Elias Bayter, farming and family have always gone hand-in-hand. They grew up watching and learning from their parents, who originally grew avocados on El Vergel Estate, a gorgeous plot of land which sits on the slope of an inactive volcano in the Tolima department of Colombia. In 2006, however, a disease severely affected the crop, and global avocado prices dropped significantly as a result.
That's when Martha, the Bayter family matriarch, turned her eyes toward coffee. In an effort to diversify their crops and save the farm, she planted several coffee varieties and started learning. In the years that followed, the family collaborated with processing enthusiasts such as Nelson Moya and varietal specialits like Miguel Jimenez, each of whom played a pivotal role in the trajectory - and legacy - of El Vergel.
Fast forward to today: Shady and Elias manage the now-modernized farm on the side of the volcano, cultivating over 28 coffee varieties and extensively researching new and innovative ways to process their storied lots. The brothers and their parents are regarded as "pioneers of innovation and quality" throughout Colombia and the coffee-growing world, and today's advanced-processed Ombligon lot is certainly a testament to their endeavors.

Since then, they’ve worked to produce world class coffees while creating greater value for the smallholder farmers they support. In Dumerso, farmers cultivate traditional Ethiopian coffee varieties high in the mountains, where cool temperatures and unique growing conditions help shape Yirgacheffe’s celebrated character. This washed lot captures the classic Yirgacheffe profile, bringing together fragrant hibiscus, delicate black tea, sweet citrus, and ripe blueberry in an elegant, expressive cup carried by a smooth, velvety mouthfeel. Mahder and Hirut’s impact extends beyond coffee quality. In a region where coffee provides more than 90% of household income, their commitment to supporting local farmers is especially meaningful. title: Café con Leche
body:
When we began doing pop-ups, we created our “almost famous” Horchata Cold Brew, which immediately became everyone’s favorite. Still to this day. This coffee reminded me of that drink. This wild, experimental, and unique coffee showcases farmer Diego Bermudez’s innovative processing skills. Nerd out on the processing method below to see how it gives a taste that will remind you of a sweet,-coconut-milky-cinnamon-tropical coffee drink!
The process of this profile begins with the careful harvesting of coffee cherries at their optimum ripeness. The cherries are then disinfected with ozone and transferred to fermentation tanks, where an anaerobic fermentation is carried out for 72 hours, submerged in water with Lactobacillus in a milk culture medium. After fermentation, the coffee is pulped and mixed with the leachates collected during the cherry fermentation, in order to increase the level of precursors in the seed. Next, a thermal shock wash is performed to fix a greater amount of precursors and seal the coffee for an optimal drying process. Drying is done in a dehumidifier to remove moisture while preserving the soft notes of the coffee, preventing over-oxidation of the seed, and halting metabolic processes to avoid over-fermentation. Finally, the coffee is stabilized, stored in a cool place, and then selected and hulled according to quality standards.

title: Kenya AA - Bungoma, Kenya
body:
Kenya AA coffee is widely considered in general to be one of the best and most iconic coffees in the world. This selection is grown at elevations between 1500 and 1900 meters above sea level (up to 6000 feet). These high growing altitudes surrounding Mount Kenya, which reaches a peak of nearly 17,000 feet and lies a mere 10 miles south of the equator, produce more mature beans grown at a slower rate allowing the flavors to develop more fully in red volcanic soil that is ultra fertile with gentle slopes that provide adequate drainage.
The AA designation of the coffee is from its grading. The Kenya coffee industry grades all beans first by size then measured immediately after processing with the size graded through a screened sieve type method. Their standard is specific to Kenya with the experience and knowledge in their region that the largest beans (AA and AA+) will be the most superior in flavor due to the climate and elevation at which they are grown.
The first thing you'll notice about this coffee is the amazing floral aromas and mild fruitiness, specifically berries. The mouth feel is a full round body that is super smooth that some relate to being lightly syrupy. A bright citrus note on first sip belies this coffee's known brightness that quickly morphs into a bit of berry sweetness, and juiciness.

Indonesia was introduced to coffee by the Dutch in the mid-seventeenth century. It is home to the first commercial coffee plantations in the world.
The first coffee production sold was in 1712 in Amsterdam, The Netherlands. Coffee production expanded well during these early days; however, in 1877, the coffee plantations were wiped out by a coffee root disease forcing the country to replant new coffee trees. Most new coffee plants came from Africa and were primarily Robusta Beans, because these were more root disease resistant. Today Indonesia is still a major producer of Robusta Beans. However 10 to 15% of the Coffees produced in Indonesia are Arabica beans. The best growing regions for the Arabica varieties are on the islands of Sumatra, Sulawesi, Java, Flores, and Bali. Indonesian Arabica beans are traditionally strong, complex flavored, with a syrupy quality and often a balanced acidity.

title: Hario Cold Brewer
body:
The Hario Mizudashi Cold Brew Coffee Pot is our favorite simple vessel for making cold brew. It's just three parts: a 1 liter glass pot, a filter basket and a lid. It's easy to use & clean up, filters well, and doesn't take up much space!
Just add 90 grams of coarsely ground coffee (we recommend our Cold Brew Blend ) to the filter basket and insert into the carafe. Fill water over the coffee grounds, stir to make sure everything is saturated, and then store in the fridge. After 12-18 hours, just pull out the filter & you're done! You can store your cold brew in the same pot you just brewed in.
You can use this for cold brew tea with the same method -- try starting with 10 grams of tea per pot!
We recommend hand washing the pot only. This is very high quality Japanese glassware, but is more prone to breaking or chipping when sent through the dishwasher.

title: SCA SENSORY SKILLS INTERMEDIATE CLASS
body:
The Sensory Skills Intermediate course builds on the concepts and skills introduced in the Sensory Skills Foundation course and prepares the learner for more complex job functions in the sensory evaluation of coffee and related products. This course covers a wide range of topics, including the physiology of taste and aroma; the types of sensory analysis tests, the operation of a cupping session; the diversity of coffee attributes; the use of the SCA Flavor Wheel and WCR Sensory Lexicon; and the implementation of a sensory analysis panel and session. A written exam tests intermediate course knowledge while a practical exam assesses the learner’s ability to identify basic differences in coffee attributes and recall fragrance identification.
This is a two-day class comprised of lecture, coursework, and hands-on practice. After passing exams, students receive a certificate of recognition by the SCA.
Note: Current holders of a valid CQI Q Grader license may qualify to waive the practical exam for this course. See your Authorized SCA Trainer for more details.
In order to register for this class, you need an SCA Learner Number. To create a free SCA Learner Number or to find your existing number, please visit here.
SCA Coffee Skills Diploma and Certification
All written exams for the SCA are hosted online and distributed via email. SCA exam and certification fees are included in the cost for tickets and are optional for students who take class recreationally.

title: Ethiopia – Shakiso Natural
body:
This naturally processed coffee from Kayon Mountain Coffee Farms has notes of strawberry and honeysuckle that will make you say Mmmmmmm!

Whole Bean | 12 oz. bag (340g)
ETHIOPIA SHAKISO NATURAL
This Shakiso Natural comes from Kayon Mountain Coffee Farm in the Shakiso district in the Guji Zone, about 530 km from Addis Ababa. The farm is owned by families that were born and raised in the area and have 30 years of coffee experience and is located in the shadows of evergreens that provide a multi-canopy structure. The Shakiso regions’ volcanic soil is bursting with nutrients, creating a deep red and brown top-layer of soil. The regions’ high altitude, bi-modal rainfall pattern, and dry weather allow coffee cherries to develop slowly.
Guji is one of the zones of the Oromia Region of Ethiopia. Guji is named after a tribe of the Oromo people. It is bordered on the south by Borena, on the west by the Southern Nations, Nationalities, and Peoples Region, on the north by the Ganale Dorya River which separates it from Bale and on the east by the Somali Region.

Region / County: Nyeri County, Central Province (Kenya)

The Heritage of Thiriku Factory
Registered as an independent cooperative society in 2000, Thiriku operates a single, highly focused wet mill (factory) nestled in the heart of Nyeri County at the foot of the Aberdare mountain range.
Benefiting from nutrient-rich volcanic soil, cool mountain nights, and altitudes pushing nearly 2,000 meters, Thiriku's smallholder farmers carefully hand-pick ripe cherries for centralized processing. Using classic Kenyan double-fermentation and raised bed drying techniques, this lot yields the signature tangy sweetness and vibrant floral notes that make Nyeri coffees world-famous.
Coffee with a Purpose: Every bag purchased provides 1 meal to someone in need through our partnership with 2nd Harvest Food Bank.

body:

From the sun-drenched hills of Ciudad Bolívar, Antioquia in Colombia, Paula 20 Brix is a standout natural-processed microlot that marries deep sweetness with fruit complexity and rich chocolate character. In the cup, this lot offers lush notes of ripe blackberry and dark chocolate, layered with hints of cognac and fine oak, culminating in a smooth, resonant finish that balances fruit depth with comforting sweetness.
Grown at 1,600–1,800 masl on Finca Santa Elena , this coffee reflects both the region’s fertile Andean soils and the farm’s meticulous approach to harvesting. Selectively hand-picked cherries are dried naturally with the whole fruit intact, allowing sugars and fruit acids to intensify and fuse with the bean during drying—yielding pronounced body and a distinctly aromatic profile.
Named for its 20° Brix sugar concentration—a measure of exceptional ripeness—this microlot highlights the careful cultivation and innovative practices of farmers Paula and Samuel, whose sustainability efforts underscore both cup quality and community impact.
With its rich fruit character, chocolate backbone, and nuanced sweetness, Paula 20 Brix is a bold yet refined natural that showcases Colombia’s specialty coffee evolution.

title: Dragon Phoenix Pearl Loose Leaf Tea
body:
Dragon Phoenix Pearl gets its name from the visual characteristics of the tea bushes "climbing" the hillsides like a Dragon coming out of the water. The tea is picked in April/May and is processed by hand, by rolling each leaf and a bud into tiny pearl size balls. Once rolled, the tea is wrapped in silk mesh and dried by fire to set the form. The tea is then held until August/September when the finest jasmine blossoms are in bloom. The two are married together and the result is amazing!
Jasmine-Scented Loose Leaf Tea
Dragon Phoenix Pearl Loose Leaf Tea brings a fragrant jasmine character to your tea collection. Its hand-rolled pearls make brewing part of the experience, gradually opening as they steep. It’s an inviting choice for tea drinkers who enjoy floral aromas or want to explore loose leaf tea beyond their everyday blend.
Prepare with a roomy tea infuser or teapot that gives the pearls space to expand, following the package instructions for water temperature, tea quantity, and steeping time. Enjoy your first cup without milk or sweetener to appreciate the jasmine fragrance, then adjust future cups to your taste.
Discover More Loose Leaf Teas
Explore Green Dragon Oolong Loose Leaf Tea for floral aromas with buttery and nutty notes. You can also browse the full Java City tea collection to discover organic hot teas, spiced chai, and caffeine-free herbal infusions.

Each 12oz bag contains 300mg of broad spectrum CBD from USDA-certified organic, USA-grown hemp, processed via winterized CO2 extraction. 0% THC.
Costa Rican coffee is known for mild acidity and a clean cup. This lot is washed processed, the cherry skin and mucilage are removed before drying, which is what produces that clean cup. Expect dark chocolate, vanilla, and almond, with a piloncillo sweetness.
Costa Rica has some of the most tightly regulated coffee production in the world. Small farms dominate the landscape, and the country was the first in Central America to completely ban the cultivation of lower-quality robusta, ensuring that every bag coming out of Costa Rica is 100% arabica. This commitment to quality is something we share. Always 100% mold free.
Third-party lab tested for CBD potency and THC absence. A small-batch offering, available while supply lasts.

body:
LOCATION SPECIFICS
Southern Huila, Colombia
ROAST DEGREE
1 rooster
ORGANIC?
No
FARMER/COOP NAME DETAILS
25 Farmers: 10 women and 15 men farmers
PROCESSING DETAILS
Pulped out of skin. Fermented submerged in tanks of water for 50 hours. Washed clean. Dried on patios and solar dryers.
COFFEE VARIETY
100% Pink Bourbon: a natural mutation of Bourbon varietal that turns a pale pink when ripe
Altitude: M.A.S.L.
1,600–1,900
About This Coffee
Our first new coffee of 2025! This is a lot made of 100% single variety: Pink Bourbon. Pink Bourbon is a natural mutation of the classic Bourbon variety. It turns a shade of pink rather than deep red when it is ripe, ready to be picked. This coffee was grown in the Palestina, Pitalito, Salado Blanco, Acevedo municipalities of Huila Colombia. It was grown by a small producer group of 10 women and 15 men. Beside growing and picking stunning cherry they are also responsible for the immaculate processing to which these coffee cherries are exposed. They employ a slightly modified version of the classic washed process with a couple of steps amended specifically to give us the result we find in this amazing coffee. These coffee cherries were first pulped from their skin then fermented under water for 50 hours. The beans are then washed clean before patio drying, finished in solar dryers. The flavors coming from this coffee are sweet, slightly exotic, and even slightly floral — a stunning example of this infrequently found coffee variety.

body:

The Secret Temple is our Ethiopian single origin — a coffee that reveals its complexity slowly, layer by layer, like exploring the rooms of an ancient temple.
TASTING NOTES
Milk chocolate, cherry, and blueberry. The first sip opens with a gentle milk chocolate sweetness, followed by ripe cherry mid-palate, and finishes with a distinctive blueberry note that Ethiopian coffees are celebrated for. This is a naturally complex coffee that needs no additions — just good water and the right brew method.
BEST BREWING METHODS
This single origin was selected specifically for pour over and drip brewing, where the delicate fruit notes can fully express themselves. We recommend a medium-fine grind and water temperature around 200°F (93°C). A Chemex or V60 pour over will give you the clearest expression of these flavors.
ORIGIN STORY
Ethiopia is the birthplace of coffee, and the beans we source reflect centuries of growing tradition. The high-altitude farms produce small, dense beans packed with flavor — the kind of coffee that reminds you why single origins exist.

title: Decaf Colombia - Pods
body:
Our Decaf Colombia is sourced from a group of women producers. This group began in 1999 by 80 women to form the AMACA. Now the AMACA is 140 smallholder members strong.
All of the members derive their livelihood from the cultivation and production of coffee. A premium is paid to AMACA above the value of the coffee in order to support their goals and aspirations as a group. Their mantra is simple: to improve the quality of life for their members and their members’ families. Currently, one of their most pressing needs is a warehouse space to properly receive, cup, manage, and store their coffees. We believe these premiums can help them to accomplish these goals and in turn, support this passionate and strong-willed group of women in their love for and livelihood of quality coffee.
Notes: Excellent flavor balance, a delicious decaf with citrus and caramel notes.
What is EA Wash?
EA wash is the process used to remove the caffeine from the bean. To remove the caffeine, sugarcane is fermented to produce Ethyl Acetate. The beans are washed through large filters (think Brita style) that extract the caffeine from the bean. Leaving behind all the good stuff (flavors, color and its true origin) of the green bean. This is a natural process of removal - chemical free.

The SSP Unimodal MP (Multi Purpose) burrs have a geometry intended to excel at highlighting flavor clarity. This style of burr tends to work better for lighter roast coffees, especially fruity natural fermented beans, but also tend to work great with medium roasts or washed beans as well. SSP MP burrs work great with coffees that have a higher acidity making the acidity in the cup more enjoyable. These multi-purpose burrs were primarily designed to be used as brew burrs, but the latest version also excels with espresso as well. These burrs are not recommended for darker roasted coffees.
SSP’s burrs are designed to last a lifetime using tool steel and coated with Red Speed Titanium Aluminum Carbon Nitride (TiAICN). On average SSP burrs have been able to grind over 10,000 pounds of coffee before needing replaced.

The terrain of Chiapas is mountainous and jagged, but provides an ideal climate to grow coffee. Chiapas is in the Southern part of Mexico and most people in the area are extremely poor and rely on coffee as a main source of income. The mountainous highlands and dense rainforest are dotted with Mayan archaeological sites and Spanish colonial towns. Chiapas is responsible for 60 percent of Mexico’s coffee production and in addition produces Cacao for export.
Most of the coffee is grown on small farms by families in one of the poorest regions of the Country. The coffee is grown at over 4000 feet in the same mountain range as the Guatemalan Huehuetenango region which produces some of the best coffee.
The Decaf Mexico is a Full City Roast coffee and has a smooth caramel flavor with a big finish.

title: ICT Ethiopia Dembi
body:
In Sidama, Ethiopia, first-generation coffee producer Solomon Hameso Boky works alongside his son and approximately 200 local farmers who deliver freshly harvested coffee cherries to his processing sites. At Dembi, Solomon cultivates coffee among established trees and enriches the soil with a thick layer of natural compost. His work also supports the surrounding community by creating employment for women, assisting local elders, and providing young coffee plants to neighboring farmers.
After harvest, the cherries are carefully sorted and naturally processed on raised African beds. Grown at elevations of 1,800–2,000 meters, Dembi produces a smooth and fruit-forward cup with lively orange citrus and sweet strawberry notes.

title: Edinson Argote - Cherry Limeade
body:
MEET THE PRODUCER | Edinson Argote has overcome tremendous odds to become the renowned, passionate coffee producer we know him to be. Orphaned at age three, Edinson was raised by his sister until he decided to leave home at age 11. For seven years, Edinson found odd jobs to support himself until he could join the army when he turned 18. When he got out of the army at 20 years old, Edinson began working for his cousin at a local coffee buying station in Acevedo, Colombia. It was there that his interest was piqued and his passion for coffee fully realized.
In 2018, Edinson and his girlfriend, Luz Angela, took a loan from her father and used it to acquire La Quebradita, a picturesque coffee farm located on the slopes of the Central Mountain Range, in Timaná. Today, La Quebradita is a hub for coffee processing and farmland innovation, experimenting with everything from yeast inoculation to soil care. Edinson has made it his life's work to produce specialty coffee using unique and replicable sensory profiles, and this blend of an advanced natural Chiroso and a washed Maragesha lot showcase his talent beautifully.
TRUST THE PROCESS | For the Chiroso lot: After being picked at peak ripeness, whole coffee cherries undergo standard natural fermentation for 72 hours before being spread out on raised beds for partial drying. These new processing methods can bring out some mighty interesting flavors and this coffee from the Worka Sakaro Washing Station is a great example. We're getting a TON of fruit culminating in a scintillating finish of chocolate cake that lingers and lingers. We often find these anaerobic coffees a bit medicinal for our taste but this one is just gorgeous.
Oodles of groups are now experimenting with various methods of anaerobic (without air) processing. It follows all the same steps as a typical naturally processed coffee, except after the coffee is floated, it is placed into special plastic bags, flushed with carbon dioxide and nitrogen gas, and monitored over 3-7 days until fermented adequately (this varies based on mucilage content and environmental conditions). Once the cherries reach the desired pH and color, they are removed from the bags and transferred to drying tables to complete the process.

ABOUT THIS COFFEE AND PRODUCER
The Anasora Site was developed with the intention of sourcing exclusive coffee from the Ethiopian highlands to deliver to specialty coffee lovers around the world. The coffee trees are intercropped and shade grown between spices, tuber crops and false banana.
For this lot, after the cherries are picked and sorted, they are left to ferment in open air for 10 hours. Then, the coffee is left to dry for 3 to 4 weeks on raised African Beds. During this drying period, the coffee is periodically turned to ensure evenness and prevent mold development.
WHY WE SELECTED THIS COFFEE
We're excited to source from the Anasora Site in Southern Guji, Ethiopia for the first time. This year's harvest caught our attention for the quality of its natural fermentation and the balance it brings to the cup.
The coffee opens with the classic berry character we often find in natural Ethiopian coffees, here it leans toward a tart but sweet blackberry. Underneath that is a bright, sweet layer of mandarin orange that remains clear throughout the cup, keeping the fermentation from becoming too dominant.

body:
We Taste - Honeysuckle, creamsicle, tropical
Efrain Carhuallocllo might be the most awarded coffee producer from Perú, which makes us very excited to share his unique microlot with you. Efrain and his wife Maria Flor are second generation coffee producers who put their hearts into El Cerro. Near the town of El Corazón, they built a small family farm nestled amongst Andean forests, where cool mountain air builds sweetness and complexity in a very special coffee variety. A rare, delicate, and low-yielding variety, Gesha comes from Ethiopia and brings with it an exquisite flavor profile. At two to three weeks off-roast, a classic Ethiopia profile emerges with aromatics of honeysuckle, creamy orange, and tropical fruit.
Efrain and Maria Flor farm as a labor of love, picking only ripe cherry, sorting for excellence in the cup, and processing at their on-site wet mill (a rarity for a farm of this size). Caring for their own processing means they go directly from field to mill, preserving the essence of the world's most sought after variety. They create even more character by extending the fermentation of their washed process. After depulping, the mucilage coffee is water soaked in tanks for 24 hours. A longer fermentation window develops tropical fruit aromatics (think mango) and creaminess in body that complements the elegant florals and sweet citrus intrinsic to a fine Gesha varietal character.
